analysis.investment_thesis: Dilip Buildcon scores reasonably on earnings yield (~13%) but fails the Magic Formula's second test with ROIC of only ~14%, well below the 20% threshold for a "good business." Persistently negative free cash flow and a ballooning debt load disqualify this as a Magic Formula candidate.
key_strengths: Earnings yield of ~13% (EBIT INR 2,159 Cr / EV ~INR 16,600 Cr) clears the >12% attractiveness threshold
Revenue CAGR of 11.6% over 9 years shows execution scale in India's infrastructure build-out
P/B of 0.98 and EV/EBITDA of 8.76 suggest the market is not pricing in a recovery — downside may be limited
key_risks: ROIC ~14% (using reported ROCE 14.8%) is below the Magic Formula's 20% floor — this is not a high-quality business by my criteria
Free cash flow has been deeply negative every single year: -INR 4,134 Cr (2025), -INR 4,473 Cr (2024), -INR 1,071 Cr (2023) — the business destroys cash relentlessly
Debt surged from INR 6,658 Cr (2023) to INR 10,375 Cr (2025); finance costs of INR 1,249 Cr consume 58% of EBIT, leaving almost nothing for equity holders after debt service
red_flags: FCF negative in all 5 observable years — capex (INR 4,265 Cr in 2025) dwarfs operating cash flow (INR 131 Cr in 2025)
FY2025 net profit of INR 840 Cr is propped up by INR 417 Cr of Other Income — strip that out and operating earnings are far weaker
Net profit turned negative in FY2022 (-INR 550 Cr) and nearly zero in FY2023 (-INR 1 Cr), revealing extreme earnings fragility and cyclicality
Debt spiked INR 3,717 Cr in a single year (FY2025), reversing years of deleveraging — signals renewed capital stress or aggressive bid book
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Dilip Buildcon, I get Earnings Yield of ~13% (EBIT INR 2,159 Cr ÷ EV of ~INR 16,600 Cr, computed as market cap INR 7,424 Cr + debt INR 9,528 Cr − cash INR 353 Cr). That clears the 12% attractiveness threshold. But the second test — Return on Capital — fails. ROCE is 14.8% against an invested capital base of ~INR 15,300 Cr (equity + debt). My formula demands 20%+; 14.8% earns no stars. An EPC infrastructure company with massive equipment, HAM project receivables, and CWIP of INR 3,164 Cr is structurally capital-hungry and can never escape the trap of low ROIC.

The cash flow picture seals the AVOID verdict. Operating cash flow in FY2025 was a paltry INR 131 Cr — down from INR 2,845 Cr in FY2023 — while capex consumed INR 4,265 Cr, resulting in FCF of negative INR 4,134 Cr. This is not a temporary dip; FCF has been negative in every year of the dataset. Finance costs of INR 1,249 Cr in FY2025 eat 58% of EBIT before a single rupee reaches equity holders. Greenblatt's formula is designed for businesses that compound capital at high rates — DBL compounds debt instead. The promoter's high 63% stake offers governance comfort, but skin-in-the-game doesn't fix a structurally low-return, cash-consuming business model.
